concept: Atlas Search index rebuild after migration
summary: Source-anchored research for Atlas Search index rebuild after migration. Run status: COMPLETED.

facts.text: Resharding requires version-specific planning. The Search FAQ says resharding removes existing search indexes and requires manual rebuilding; SERVER-120851 instead records a protective change to abort resharding when search indexes exist and require users to drop them first. The issue lists fix version 9.0.0-rc0 and requested backports, not proof of every deployed Atlas version. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/faq.md ; https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-120851

Atlas live migration does not migrate Search indexes, so the destination indexes must be built after migration. Atlas's own description of a full Search index build is that it reads the entire source collection, which may take a long time and burdens the source cluster's read operations. The reported 14x rebuild speedup comes from MongoDB's internal tests of S3-snapshot-based rebuilds on dedicated Search Nodes and should not be applied as a migration-wide savings multiplier. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration.md ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/apn/improving-mongodb-atlas-search-elasticity-with-amazon-s3/

Manning recommends free disk space of at least 125% of the current index size for background reindexing. This is headroom for replacing an existing index, not a universal estimate for an empty destination cluster. (low confidence)

An index-definition update builds a replacement in the background while the old index serves queries. A newly created destination index has no such old generation and cannot serve queries until its first build completes. Rebuild availability therefore depends on the operation. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Check the replacement definition and generation as well as queryability before accepting an index update. KnownPath records a concrete failure mode: an existing index name and a queryable old generation did not establish that the required tenant-filter definition was current. Its remediation required the latest generation to be READY and queryable. (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

LightRAG issue 3978 reports a separate recovery pitfall: its MongoDB adapter deleted documents but retained the Atlas search-index definition, causing a dimension guard to fail again during recovery. The issue calls for explicit index replacement in that application path. This is evidence about application recovery tooling, not proof that ordinary cluster migrations require embedding regeneration. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

For M10+ dedicated clusters, Cloud Backup restores search-index definitions rather than search-index data. mongot then initial-syncs the restored definitions; large indexes can delay restoration. This path differs from mongosync, which does not synchronize Search indexes. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/faq.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/limitations.md

mongosync does not synchronize Atlas Search indexes. Destination search-index creation and readiness therefore need a separate migration step; copying collection data is insufficient. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

A reply in MongoDB's community forum advised building destination search indexes after live-migration cutover in October 2024. Building during synchronization was possible, but did not guarantee consistent search results immediately after cutover. This is dated migration guidance, not evidence of a universal 2026 rebuild rule. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

Search Node scaling need not always rebuild indexes by rereading the entire source collection. MongoDB documents reuse of recent object-storage index copies for eligible dedicated Search Nodes without customer-managed Encryption at Rest; the AWS/MongoDB implementation description explains snapshot download and catch-up, with full rebuild fallback if download fails. These mechanisms do not establish cross-cluster live-migration index transfer. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31) Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/performance/index-performance.md ; https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/apn/improving-mongodb-atlas-search-elasticity-with-amazon-s3/ ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/atlas/live-migration.md

mongosync does not sync Atlas Search indexes, so destination Search indexes must be built separately from database transfer. Restored or newly built indexes require an initial sync, and large search indexes can cause delays. No source gives a general rebuild duration or dollar cost, so measure them on the intended corpus and index definition. Sources: https://www.mongodb.com/docs/mongosync/current/reference/limitations.md ; https://www.mongodb.com/docs/search/faq.md

Atlas live migration does not migrate MongoDB Search indexes from the source cluster to the destination. Destination Search index creation must be planned separately from document migration. (high confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)

The April 2, 2025 AWS/MongoDB article reports a 14-fold index reconstruction speed improvement in MongoDB internal tests using S3 snapshots. It does not provide an independently reproduced migration benchmark or a guaranteed cross-cluster cutover duration. (low confidence) (verified as of 2026-10-31)
